rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 1-2 report the authors' own replicated field experiments (RCBD, four replications, two locations in NC, summer 2018) comparing a UAV weed-mapping plus UAV-spraying system (UAV-IS) with ground-based broadcast applications.
rows.notes: The study maps weeds with UAV imagery and uses the maps for site-specific herbicide application; it reports area sprayed, precision, recall, application efficiency and herbicide injury on weeds. It does not measure crop productivity, yield or any sustainability outcome; trials were on out-of-production or weed-free sod fields with no crop. It does show reduced area treated (20-60% less), which bears on resource (herbicide) efficiency, but the claimed effect on crop productivity is not evaluated, so the study supports only a precondition (efficient weed detection and treatment) of the productivity claim. Nothing in the study tests 'scalable, rapid, repeatable monitoring' as such beyond a single season of plot-scale mapping.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3, Tables 1-2: own replicated field experiments at two NC locations in 2018. Q2: Section 2.2-2.3 and Fig. 2: UAV orthomosaics classified into weed maps used to build prescription flight maps for a UAV sprayer; Tables 1-2 and Sections 3.1-3.2: UAV-IS treated 77% vs 98% (natural weeds) and 33% vs 93% (surrogate weeds) of plot area, i.e. 20-60% less area sprayed, treated only 30% of non-weedy area versus 92% for broadcast, with application efficiency 19% higher and three times higher respectively; herbicide injury on tobacco surrogates was higher with UAV-IS (Table 2) and 15-16% lower on K. striata (Table 1). Q4: Tables 1-2 and Section 2.4: the intermediate variables (area sprayed, false positives on non-weedy area, false negatives, precision, recall, F score) were quantified by overlaying weed-detection maps with post-application injury maps; detection accuracy of the classification verified at <1% error (Section 2.2). Q7: Section 3.2 and Conclusion: authors state from their results that the application efficiency gain depends on weed spatial aggregation, that the surrogate-weed advantage was favored by high aggregation, and that pesticide reduction applies where weed distribution is clearly aggregated and broadcast applications are not justified; impact on efficacy depends on weed distribution and morphology. Q8: Section 3.3: UAV sprayer deviated up to 1 m from target due to GPS accuracy without RTK and wind; UAV-IS missed up to 26% of target weedy area (Sections 3.1-3.2); Section 2.2: flight-path and patch-size criteria acknowledged as arbitrary; Conclusion: current system requires several software and technical processes challenging for applicators; Section 3.4: payload and battery limits make it unlikely to replace broadcast systems in large-scale operations.
rows.notes: Q2 yes for the herbicide-saving and reduced off-target (non-weedy area) treatment part of the claim; the study does not test mechanical control and does not measure operational costs or environmental impact directly, only the reduction in treated area. Q3: injury maps from post-treatment UAV imagery were visually verified on the ground and tobacco dry weight was measured, but the central result (area sprayed, precision/recall) rests on one image-overlay method with ground checking rather than two independent methods; rated no with some doubt. Q5: two locations (Candor sand; Gritney/Wedowee sandy loam), both NC sod fields, results reported for two weed scenarios only. Q6: plots of 100-136 m2. Q9: Tables give means and P values only, no SD, SE or CI.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a plot-scale field evaluation of integrated UAV weed mapping and UAV site-specific glufosinate application versus backpack broadcast spraying on sod fields in North Carolina; no crop yield was measured.
